newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open higher, dollar strength cited.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open higher, dollar strength cited.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened higher on Monday, getting a lift from a strong dollar, analysts said.
"There was some buying associated with the dollar-yen pushing up to 114 last night," said Josh Stiles, analyst at I.D.E.A.
The dollar opened in New York at three-and-a-half-year highs against the yen.
Analysts said swap activity related to some eurobond issues also created some demand for U.S. Treasuries overnight.
"There was good interest in three-, five- and 10-year notes, partly related to swap activity from a number of eurobond issues," said Kim Rupert, analyst at MMS International.
Stiles said the market has a positive bias coming out of its performance on Friday.
Also lending support is the market's expectation for "fairly friendly" data early in the week.
"We get a lot of information this week starting Tuesday with the ECI (Employment Cost Index)," said Rupert. "That's going to be pretty important for the market."
Rupert said a 0.7 percent rise in the civilian employment cost index quarter over quarter "would be acceptable" for the market.
"A 0.8 percent rise would mean moderate trouble and a 0.9 percent gain would be pretty negative," she said.
A Reuters poll of economists culled an average forecast for the third-quarter ECI of up 0.8 percent.
"A 0.8 percent rise would be neutral for the market," said Stiles. "One percent or more would make the market very uneasy."

The market gets third-quarter GDP (Gross Domestic Product) on Wednesday. GDP is expected to be up 1.8 percent for the quarter, a very pronounced moderation from the 4.7 percent pace that prevailed in the second quarter.
Rupert contended that the GDP data would not be that important for the market.
"We already know the third quarter moderated quite a bit so that news shouldn't be much of a market factor," she said.
"The market is hoping for a neutral ECI and a bullish GDP," said Stiles. "Then people will get out before the refunding and the election."
"Could the market push up a point from here?" Stiles asked. "Yes, but it would be a selling opportunity."
On the market's mind throughout the week will be the data due Friday, the October employment data and NAPM (National Association of Purchasing Management) report.
Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that payrolls expanded by 212,000 jobs in October after losing 40,000 jobs in September.
MMS International estimates payrolls expanded by 175,000 jobs in October.
"That would definitely be market friendly," said Rupert.
In early trade, two-year notes were up 1/32 to 99-31/32, yielding 5.89 percent. Five-year notes were up 1/32 to 99-31/32, yielding 6.26 percent.
The 6-1/2 percent ten-year note was unchanged at 99-23/32, yielding 6.54 percent.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond was up 4/32 in its initial trades but eased to unchanged levels soon after. At 99-5/32, it was yielding 6.82 percent.
Three- and six-month bill rates were unchanged at 4.99 percent and 5.11 percent, respectively. Year bill rates were down one basis point to 5.23 percent.
-- North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679
